title: Environmental recurrence selects a costly memory-use policy: long-run population effects and immediate retrieval effects
description: Three accepted prospective long-run computational studies show recurrence-attributable enrichment of a costly supplied-cache-use policy, with population-performance contrasts bounded below declared positive scales or unresolved. The subsequent BIT002 identical-state, one-turnover retrieval experiment uses 42,000 independent new BIT/PL histories. At recurrent targets, cached retrieval materially increased eligible-lineage survivor share and unconditional focal-family contribution, and increased normalized accuracy with magnitude unresolved. All three innovation-target effects were bounded within prespecified margins, with negative estimates and zero-containing intervals; bounds do not establish absence. All six estimates, exact intervals and original adverse/bounded/unresolved findings are retained. Immediate effects do not establish long-run mediation, a recurrence intervention, TORUS retrieval effects or biological memory. Only 64 factual histories were independently replayed; conditional state provenance limits remain explicit. Internal AI-assisted reviews are not external peer review.
